content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present a new method for causal transfer learning based on task affinity frameworks. They derive a new metric which is able to measure the similarity between two causal inference tasks. They show how this contribution is able to transfer knowledge from 'close' tasks to the present one, reducing the need for training data by as much as "95%" in some cases.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This is the main review. It proceeds according to the section headings of your paper.

## Abstract

- I appreciate that you have a lot to say but the abstract is meant to be but a brief summary of your method and results. Please compress it, it is too detailed for a quick 'skim' (which is what a lot of your readers will be doing -- if it is too long they will not even bother, so it is a fine balance to strike).

## Introduction

- You make a lot of (interesting) claims in the first paragraph but do not a single reference for any one of them. Transportability is a well-studied concept in causal inference (and as 'transfer learning' outside of causal inference too, as your second paragraph demonstrates). To lend some credence to the start of your paper, please furnish it with more sources to add some veracity to your narrative.
- In particular, you say "natural neural systems can intuitively determine the similarity of scenarios and estimate average gains of action in a new scenario from those of past experiences" - that is a very large claim which at present is unsupported.
- I like your camel and horses example. Very well put.
- Nitpicking, figure 1: the quotation marks around 'flipped' should be done using `` and '' to properly render in latex.
- Sentence construction, legend, figure 1: "we cannot have validation dataset" --> 'we are not in possession of a validation dataset'.
- What you are talking about in figure 1 and paragraph 2 of this section is known as  _the fundamental problem of causal inference_ (Rubin 1974; Holland 1986). You should mention that for consistency and indexing.
- Shouldn't your causal diagrams be different in figure 2 if they are indeed different tasks? What similarity are you measuring if they are the same causal diagram?
- In item three you say: "These bounds formally imply transferability for causal knowledge." - that is an odd sentence, could you explain better what you mean? It sounds as if the existence of the bounds implies that causal knowledge can de facto be transported. 

## Related work

- The structure of your paper lends itself well to placing the related work _after_ your contributions (method/theory etc). It will improve the flow of the paper. 
- Transfer learning goes back much further than recent applications to neural networks. Sebastian Thrun discussed it as early as 1997. My meaning is that don't get too overly focused on deep learning utility and be aware that it is a much more general concept.
- Very comprehensive, well done.

## Mathematical background

- What is a causal inference dataset? Is there a source? Do you mean observational data (sampled without the influence of an intervention)? Is there a source for this background?
- $T=0$ is your observational setting then, the empty-set intervention or no intervention (this is the do-calculus perspective).
- How should we thinking about treatment assignment when $M > 1$ - is this the setting where multiple types of treatments are assigned rather than then binary case where it is either or?
- Provide a source for definition 1.
- Provide a source for definition 2 (unless it is a novel contribution in which case you should state this clearly).
- It would be cleaner if you separated the factual and the counterfactual loss into two separate definitions.
- Give the losses equation numbers so that they can properly referenced.
- It is very confusing that the factual loss for the treatment and control renders a different expression, compared to the factual loss definition higher up in the definition. Where does the conditional probability come from? Why is it not defined as such in first definition of the loss? In this setting, if I have understood correctly, you are defining the integral over the measured space $\mathcal{X} \times \{0,1\} \times \mathcal{Y}$ where $M = \{0,1\}$. Is that correct? So you are defining the loss function for the binary case rather than the more general case $M$?
- You say the PEHE is "often used as the performance metric for estimation of ITEs" - do you have a source or sources for this?
- Please give the IPM an equation number.
- What is the class of functions in G, in the IPM?
- Give a source for definition 4 and equation 3.
- If you use \text{TAS} in math-mode latex will render it nicer than if you simply write $TAS$ as the engine interprets the letters as variables and hence italicises them.

Lest I have missed something your contribution starts on page 6. Consequently you have spent this space introducing, reviewing and providing the necessary tools for your method. I would suggest that this is not a good use of space and that you should considerably revise the layout of the manuscript. It is not useful for your own method to have 2/3 of the paper spent on topics which are not your method and contributions. You can compress a lot of your sections, remove some definitions (and just provide a source if you go down that route) - I also recommend that you re-write the body to be more compressed and less verbose. You can also move a lot of items (e.g. definitions) to the appendix.

## PROPOSED METHOD AND TRANSFERABILITY

- Why do all tasks have the same treatment labels?
- Where does $\Psi$ come from in assumption 2; what _is_ $\Psi$?

 ## Experimental results

- Redo the legend for table 1 in the format 'total number of tasks for the dataset (#task)' it will be less cluttered and easier for the reader. 
- For figure 3, it would be helpful to know what a good trend should look like. Is it good that all alphas lie on the line $y=x$ in figure 3 (RKHS)?
- What does it mean for the balancing weights in figure 3 (movement) to overlap? Similarly for heat.
- Your figures are difficult to interpret with the current explanation that goes with them. It is not immediately clear what one should be looking for (or what one should not be looking) in order to make a useful judgement as to validity/utillity of your proposed method. Perhaps if you picked one dataset and described it in much more detail it would be more clear what you are trying to show.
- Table 2 is much more understandable than the figures. I would suggest you lead with that and then go with the figures.
- Change the legend for table 2 using the same recommendation as for table 1.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity

The paper is very densely written. There is a lot of material required to understand the method that the authors are proposing. I would recommend a rewrite to make the narrative easier to follow and move material around which is not necessary to understand the main contribution. 

## Quality

The writing and figures are of high quality but the narrative and exposition are, as said, difficult to follow owing to the copy-editing choices the authors have made.

## Novelty

Difficult to measure since they do not compare to any other method. Though the results are impressive (especially table 2) it is hard to say if similar results could have been found using another method.

## Reproducibility 

The authors have not mentioned the release of any implementation nor code, consequently, this work is at present not reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: An interesting paper and method but which suffers from poor copy editing, dense narrative and over-reliance on definitions which oftentimes do nothing for the method save for reducing the amount of space which could have been spent of exposing the contribution and making better experiments.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer zZ6y,

Thank you for your thoughtful review and important questions. Following your valuable comments, we have added more detailed descriptions and additional references, compressed the abstract, and modified the paper’s structure to improve its narrative.

> **Question:** “(Novelty) Difficult to measure since they do not compare to any other method. (Reproducibility) The authors have not mentioned the release of any implementation nor code.”

Causal knowledge transfer is entirely new, and no clear baseline for comparison exists. Thus, we only compared our method with one baseline (i.e., the training from scratch for the best model candidate).  Following comments of Reviewer 8LDE, we have also included the comparison of our results to models trained with bundled data sets, which further demonstrates significant gains of our approach. Additionally, our code was uploaded as the supplementary material with the submission of the manuscript. We address your other concerns individually below.

> **Question:** “You make a lot of (interesting) claims in the first paragraph but do not a single reference for any one of them…”

We have updated our manuscript to include more references and a discussion about transportability. Transportability is a well-studied concept in causal discovery, however, it is different from causal transfer learning. Transportability tackles the question of transferring **casual relationships** in the do-calculus framework. Here, we are interested in transferring **knowledge of Individual Treatment Effects** from a source task to a target task in the Neyman-Rubin framework using representation learning. In other words, the causal relationships are the same across tasks in our setting; we try to transfer the knowledge of outcome functions from source to target tasks.

> **Question:** “Shouldn't your causal diagrams be different in figure 2 if they are indeed different tasks? What similarity are you measuring if they are the same causal diagram?”

In Figure 2, the causal diagrams represent neural network models for estimating the causal effects, and not the causal relationships. In our transfer learning scenarios, we only transfer between tasks with the same causal graph. The difference between causal inference problems originates from the features, treatment, and outcome distribution. 

> **Question:** “In item three you say: "These bounds formally imply transferability for causal knowledge." - that is an odd sentence, could you explain better what you mean? It sounds as if the existence of the bounds implies that causal knowledge can de facto be transported.”

These bounds indicate that the counterfactual loss and the performance (i.e. $\epsilon_{PEHE}$) of the target task are bounded by the factual loss of the source task and other measurable quantities. With a related source task (i.e., Assumption 4 for the main theorem), both the target task’s factual and counterfactual performances are guaranteed. Therefore, we have the transferability of causal knowledge.

> **Question:** “What is a causal inference dataset? Is there a source? Do you mean observational data (sampled without the influence of an intervention)? Is there a source for this background?”

Yes, you are absolutely right. A causal inference dataset is an observational dataset sampled from a tuple of random variables $(X,T,Y)$ (where no intervention is done). For example, in the medical case $X$ can be the features of an individual, $T$ the vaccine, and Y the mortality outcome. For a treatment variable $T \in \{0,1\}$, the group with $T=0$  could be the group who didn’t receive the vaccine, and the group with $T=1$ is the group who received the vaccine. This setup is similar to $\text{(Johanson et al 2016, page 2)}^{[1]}$ and $\text{(Shalit et al 2017, page 4)}^{[2]}$.

> **Question:** “How should we thinking about treatment assignment when M>1 ..”

M > 1 means that there are more than 2 possible treatments. For instance, if we studied the effect of educational level on income level, we would have more than 2 categories (e.g., high school graduate, undergraduate degree, graduate degree, etc.) as multiple treatment groups (in this case M > 1).

content.title: Continuation
content.comment:
> **Question:** “It is very confusing that the factual loss for the treatment and control renders a different expression, compared to the factual loss definition higher up in the definition...“

Yes, we consider the measurable space $\mathcal{X}\times${$0,1$}$\times\{Y}$ since we assumed without loss of generality that M=1. If M>1, then the measurable space will be $\mathcal{X}\times${$0,\ldots,M$}$\times\mathcal{Y}$. Let us consider an example from the medical field (where M=1), the individuals’ features (e.g., age, sex, etc..) are in some space $\mathcal{X}$, the treatment variable $T \in${$0,1$} can represent whether the individual has received vaccine A or vaccine B, and Y can model the mortality outcome. The factual loss for the entire population is defined over the joint distribution. If we take each group separately (e.g., those who had received vaccine A), then the joint distribution of the features and the outcome is the conditional distribution $p(x,y|t= \text{vaccine A})$. Based on your comment, we have added this example to the Appendix (see Section 8.2).

> **Question:** “What is the class of functions in G, in the IPM?”

Mathematically, G (in the IPM definition) can be any class of measurable functions. In our paper, we have considered the case where G is the set of 1-Lipschitz functions, and in this case, the IPM corresponds to the 1-Wasserstein distance by the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality result.

> **Question:** “Why do all tasks have the same treatment labels?”

In this paper, we have considered the case where the treatment assignments have the same cardinalities. Extension to varying sizes of cardinalities is a very interesting yet challenging question that we plan to consider in subsequent future work. Thank you for your thoughtful comment.
> **Question:** “Where does $\Psi$ come from in assumption 2?”

$\Psi$ is defined in Assumption 2 as the inverse of the feature function $\Phi$. $\Phi$ is the representation learning network defined in Section 3.

> **Question:** “For figure 3, it would be helpful to know what a good trend should look like. Is it good that all alphas lie on the line..”

Thank you for your comment. In Figure 3, we expect to observe a strong correlation between the task distance (on the x-axis) and the counterfactual loss (on the y-axis). **Thus, a straight line is ideal.** The observation that all alphas lie on the line shows the proposed task affinity’s robustness to variations of the hyper-parameters. We have added this explanation to the updated manuscript. Thank you again for your thoughtful questions.

> **Question:** “What does it mean for the balancing weights in figure 3 (movement) to overlap? Similarly for heat..”

The balancing weight is an important hyper-parameter for the causal inference model. Hyper-parameters’ values can be cross-validated on the validation set in common transfer learning scenarios. However, in causal inference problems where no validation data can be accessed, the choice of hyper-parameters is solely based on assumptions and educated guesses. The overlapping behaviors of distance/counterfactual loss under different balancing weights show that the proposed distance is robust to the choice of hyper-parameters. This is a highly desirable property. 

---

[1] Johansson, F., Shalit, U., & Sontag, D. (2016, June). Learning representations for counterfactual inference. In International conference on machine learning (pp. 3020-3029). PMLR.

[2] Shalit, U., Johansson, F. D., & Sontag, D. (2017, July). Estimating individual treatment effect: generalization bounds and algorithms. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 3076-3085). PMLR.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to leverage transfer learning in the estimation of individual treatment effect (ITE) through representation learning, building on the TARNet approach developed by Shalit et al. (2016). The main contributions include a proposed measure of task affinity, some results on upper bounds of errors in the proposed approach, and empirical demonstrations of the reasonableness of the proposed task affinity measure and of the gain in sample efficiency.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The topic is interesting and important.
2. The paper presents both theoretical and empirical results (though they are not very tightly linked, see below.) 
3. The gain in sample efficiency as shown in experiments is significant. 

Weaknesses:

1. The theoretical results have quite limited originality and significance. The originality is limited, because as far as I can see, they are very simple adaptations of Shalit et al.'s results. The significance is limited because they involve the unknown parameter \delta (introduced in Assumption 4), and it is unclear how we can empirically estimate or get a handle on this parameter. (Is it supposed to be somehow related to the task affinity measure?)  
2. The explanation of the rationale for symmetrizing the task affinity score is not sufficient. I am a little puzzled by the following remark in the abstract: "... the absolute values of ITEs are invariant under the action of the symmetric group on the labels of treatments. Given this invariance, we propose a symmetrized task distance for calculating the similarity of a target scenario with those encountered before." I am not sure why this invariance justifies or motivates the symmetrization, and I fail to find a discussion of this point in the main text. In any case, I think it would be helpful to compare the symmetrized and the unsymmetrized score, at least empirically. In the current paper, I don't find much insight or evidence regarding why the original, unsymmetrized task affinity score is less attractive than the measure proposed in this paper.  
3. The connection between the theoretical results and the empirical studies seems rather loose. The theoretical upper bounds do not seem to be featured in any way in the experiments. I thought the proposed task affinity measure might be used to test Assumption 4 or indicate the value of \delta in Assumption 4, but I don't see such experimental results. On the other hand, there is no theoretical analysis of the expected gain in sample efficiency, as shown in the empirical results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The originality of the work is acceptable but not great. The symmetrizing idea seems to be the most novel bit, but its justification is a little too sketchy. The clarity could be improved. In addition to the lack of explanation of the motivation or rationale for the proposed measure of task distance, the methods actually used in the paper to estimate the task distance and to estimate the ITEs in the target task could be more clearly described. As it stands now, I am not sure how easy it is to reproduce the results. There are also some minor puzzling statements. For example, the statement of conditional unconfoundedness in the middle of p. 4 seems to me to be a mistake. At the bottom of p. 4, the direct identification of "small factual and counterfactual losses" with "low \epsilon_{PEHE}" is also confusing. Moreover, on p. 6, in the definition of the label-invariant task affinity distance, should F_{a, b} be F_{a, a} instead, as in Definition 5?
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper tackles an interesting problem, with some promising empirical results. However, the theoretical part has limited significance and its connection to the proposed methodology and the empirical results is not entirely clear.

content.title: Connection between Theory and Experiments; Novelty and Significance of the Proposed Theories; Rationale for the Symmetrized Task Distance
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer VAjN, 

Thank you for your constructive review and questions. Following your valuable comments, we have added more detailed descriptions and pseudocode of the proposed task distance, fixed the typos, and conducted additional experiments to compare the symmetrized and the un-symmetrized task distance (in the Appendix). Next, we address your other concerns individually below.

> **Question:** “ The connection between the theoretical results and the empirical studies seems rather loose…”

We first analyze the transferability of causal knowledge by presenting performance guarantees (i.e., regret bounds) under general transfer learning scenarios. In the experiments, we verify that using transfer learning from a good source can significantly reduce the amount of the required training data. When we have multiple source tasks to choose from, the regret bound cannot be used as a direct method to choose. Hence, we propose a task affinity to select the closest source task to the target task. In the experiments, we verify that the proposed task affinity has the desired properties (i.e., it identifies the symmetries within the causal inference tasks.

> **Question:** “The theoretical results have quite limited originality and significance…”

Similar to many mathematical proofs, we build up from prior results of the field. Here, we prove Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 which demonstrate the upper bounds for the factual and counterfactual losses of the **target task** using the **source task’s** factual loss and other measurable quantities. We believe that this result is fundamental, and the derivation method is novel. 

There exists four important losses in transfer learning for causal inference problems:
- Factual loss of the source task (measurable)
- Counterfactual loss of the source task (unmeasurable)
- Factual loss of the target task (measurable)
- Counterfactual loss of the target task (unmeasurable)

While $\text{(Shalit et al., 2016)}^{[1]}$ has established the relationship between the factual loss and the counterfactual loss of the **same** task, our work connects the factual loss/counterfactual loss **across different tasks**. This work is analogous to the well-known regret bounds $\text{(Ben-David et al., 2010)}^{[2]}$ for discriminative classification models. To this end, we have shown that transfer learning for causal inference has a performance guarantee (i.e. regret upper bound). This upper bound provides us with a sufficient condition for transfer learning in causal inference. 

> **Question:** ''On the other hand, there is no theoretical analysis of the expected gain in sample efficiency, as shown in the empirical results.''

We are not aware of any practical approach in transfer learning for which such an analysis has been performed. We would appreciate it if you could share any prior literature and approaches to this problem.

> **Question:** “The explanation of the rationale for symmetrizing the task affinity score is not sufficient…”

Causal inference tasks can be considered as having multiple regression problems, one for each treatment group. Given a source task, if we alternate the treatment labels (i.e., 0 to 1 and 1 to 0), the treatment effect (i.e., $\mathbb{E} [Y_1-Y_0|X]$ ) will be negated. 
Consequently, the unsymmetrized task distance $\text{(Le et al., 2021)}^{[3]}$ between the original task and the permuted task can be very large. However, the original model doesn't need to be retrained for transfer learning as we only need to permute the roles of output layers of the model in order to predict the individual treatment effects correctly for each group. In other words, the causal distance between these two permuted tasks must be zero. The proposed label-invariant task affinity lends itself to this property of causal inference tasks. We also included in the Appendix a comparison between the unsymmetrized task distance and the symmetrized one (Section 8.7.1 in the Appendix). 

> **Question:** ''The significance is limited because they involve the unknown parameter \delta (introduced in Assumption 4), and it is unclear how we can empirically estimate or get a handle on this parameter. (Is it supposed to be somehow related to the task affinity measure?)''

In Assumption 4, IPM distance between the source and the target outcomes must be “reasonably close” for transfer learning to work.  Otherwise, transfer learning is not practical and may degrade the model’s performance. The value of parameter $\delta$ is important for transfer learning to work in practice. In some cases, it is possible to analyze this $\delta$ analytically. E.g., if the IPM is given by the Wassterstein distance and both $P(Y^{Ta}|X)$ and $P(Y^{Sr}|X)$ are Gaussian distributions, a closed form expression for $\delta$ can be derived. In general, empirical measurement of $\delta$ can  be challenging. However, this does not have any impact on the proposed Algorithm for causal transfer learning.

content.comment:
> **Question:** ''the methods actually used in the paper to estimate the task distance and to estimate the ITEs in the target task could be more clearly described.''

In this paper, ITEs for the synthetic datasets are given. We do not estimate ITEs for real-world datasets as we have only used these datasets to validate the proposed task affinity.

> **Question:** ''The statement of conditional unconfoundedness in the middle of p. 4 seems to me to be a mistake.''

Although the statement we wrote is true under unconfoundedness, we understand that it is not the common definition of conditional unconfoundedness in causal inference literature. We update our definition to match that presented in the literature. 

> **Question:** ''At the bottom of p. 4, the direct identification of "small factual and counterfactual losses" with "low \epsilon_{PEHE}" is also confusing. Moreover, on p. 6, in the definition of the label-invariant task affinity distance, should F_{a, b} be F_{a, a} instead, as in Definition 5''

These were typos and we have fixed them in the updated manuscript. Thank you for pointing them out!

---

[1] Shalit, U., Johansson, F. D., & Sontag, D. (2017, July). Estimating individual treatment effect: generalization bounds and algorithms. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 3076-3085). PMLR.

[2] Ben-David, S., Blitzer, J., Crammer, K., Kulesza, A., Pereira, F., & Vaughan, J. W. (2010). A theory of learning from different domains. Machine learning, 79(1), 151-175.

[3] Le, C. P., Dong, J., Soltani, M., & Tarokh, V. (2021). Task Affinity with Maximum Bipartite Matching in Few-Shot Learning. In International Conference on Learning Representations.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper combines ideas from representation learning for the estimation of conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) with tools for analysing and designing transfer learning algorithms. Theory that builds on previous results is presented, along with numerical experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Knowing how to leverage data from different distributions is always relevant when sample sizes are limited, and given the challenges of causal inference, it is important to tap into existing ideas such as transfer learning.

The combination of ideas of task-affinity measures and representation learning for CATE is a fruitful direction.

However, there doesn't seem that much work was necessary to provide a direct combination. Also, there are so many other off-the-shelf ideas that could be exploited. For instance, when only the propensity score is changing among tasks, we could literally just bundle all data together in one big regression. Maybe it's not the optimal thing to do, but surely a baseline to consider.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I had some difficulties appreciating the label-invariant task affinity construction. In fact, it wasn't clear to me what the different tasks amount to. From Appendix 7.1, it looks like that a task amounts to a different propensity score or outcome model in the experiments? As a matter of fact, I can't understand some of the datasets. What is the (binary?) treatment in "Movement (Physics)", and what are m and k? Why are the "potential outcome functions" in "Twins" changing?

I'm not sure why the permutation used in distance metric in 4.1 is particularly relevant. In any case, I have issues with (4) and (5) themselves.

It is mentioned in Definition 4 that the Fisher Information Matrix is asymptotically well-defined (under some conditions?), which I take that it means being positive definite (which is a standard result). I'm not sure whether (4) is p.d. for finite data without the sample size being at least as large as the number of parameters. Also, given that neural nets are not identifiable (at the very least due to permutations, but in general by having the ability of achieving zero training error if large enough), I'm not sure how meaningful (5) is.
content.summary_of_the_review: A relevant take on combining an existing deep learning approach for CATE estimation with a framework for transfer learning. The theory seems a bit incremental. I found the exposition hard to follow, and more convincing baselines could be used in the experiments.

content.title: Novelty and Significance of the Proposed Theories; Extra Baselines
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer 8LDE,

Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comments. Following your valuable suggestions, we have added more detailed descriptions and conducted additional experiments to improve the exposition of the paper (Please see the additional experiments in Section 8.6 in the Appendix).


> **Question:** "The theory seems a bit incremental…" 

Here, similar to many mathematical proofs, we build up from prior results in the field. We prove Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 which demonstrate the upper bounds for the factual and counterfactual losses of the **target task** using the **source task’s** factual loss and other measurable quantities. We believe that this result is fundamental, and the derivation method is novel. Thus, we respectfully disagree with your comment. 

> **Question:** "I'm not sure why the permutation used in distance metric in 4.1 is particularly relevant." 

Causal inference tasks can be considered as having multiple regression problems, one for each treatment group.  Given a source task, if we alternate the treatment labels (i.e., 0 to 1 and 1 to 0), the treatment effect (i.e., $\mathbb{E}[Y_1-Y_0|X]$) will be negated. Consequently, the unsymmetrized task distance (Le et al., 2021) between the original task and the permuted task can be very large. However, the original model doesn't need to be retrained for transfer learning as we only need to permute the roles of output layers of the model to predict the individual treatment effects correctly for each group. In other words, the task distance between these two permuted tasks must be zero. The proposed label-invariant task affinity lends itself to this property of causal inference tasks. 

In fact, to further clarify this issue, we have compared the impact of the symmetrized and un-symmetrized task distances in the Appendix (Please see Figure 7 in The Appendix). **As it can be seen the unsymmetrized task distance fails to capture the properties of Neyman-Rubin Causality.**

> **Question:** “Also, there are so many other off-the-shelf ideas that could be exploited. For instance, when only the propensity score is changing among tasks, we could literally just bundle all data together in one big regression.”

In many causal inference problems, the data is often very limited (e.g., due to privacy reasons).  Here, the prior knowledge can be used to make more concrete and accurate deductions. Moreover, we usually only have access to the trained model (e.g., in medical applications, the prior data is not available). Consequently, bundling the source tasks’ datasets may not be feasible. 

Even if the data is available, bundling datasets may  be beneficial only if the outcome functions (i.e., models) are identical (which may not be true in general). In the situation where the prior datasets are available, we have added the performance comparison between our approach and the bundling datasets method (Section 8.6 in the Appendix).  **We have compared our approach and the data bundling method on the Movement (Physics) and the IHDP dataset.** Below is the description of the results (also now added to the paper) :

1. When both propensity scores and outcomes can vary from a data-set to another, we observe that **our method outperforms the bundling method significantly** (Please see Figure 5 in the Appendix). 
2. Even when the potential outcomes are identical, our experiment in the supplementary material shows that **our approach has better performance**  with a 5% to 10% gain in different simulations (Please see Figure 6 in the Appendix). 

In summary: The bundling method has poor performance due to data imbalance, lack of precision in determining similarity from propensity score, and differences in outcome functions.

content.comment:
> **Question:** ''In fact, it wasn't clear to me what the different tasks amount to. From Appendix 7.1, it looks like that a task amounts to a different propensity score or outcome model in the experiments? As a matter of fact, I can't understand some of the datasets.''

In our experiments, we consider the scenario where both propensity scores and the outcome models are different across tasks. For instance, in the Movement (Physics) dataset, different tasks’ outcome functions have different parameters. Therefore, the outcome functions in different tasks are different.
In the Movement (Physics) dataset, each task has two treatment groups corresponding to two different values of $C=\frac{k}{m}$, where $m$ is the mass and $k$ is the air resistance. Different tasks correspond to different amounts of change in mass and air resistance. Different values of $C$ determine different potential outcome models. 
In the Twins dataset, we change the treatment label with probability $p \in (0,1) $ (without any change to the individual outcome). Hence, both the propensity score and the function relating $t$ and $x$ to $y$ are modified.

We regret that the reviewer misunderstood our contributions.  We have updated the manuscript and provided more detailed descriptions of the datasets and the process to generate them (please refer to the Appendix in the updated manuscript). We hope these details are helpful.


> **Question:** “In any case, I have issues with (4) and (5) themselves…”

In our setting, the Fisher information matrix is defined as $\mathbb{E}_{D}\big[\nabla L(\theta,D)\nabla L(\theta,D)^T \big]$
(please see Equation (9)). 

The empirical Fisher Information Matrix given in Equation (10) is positive semi-definite because it is the summation of positive semi-definite matrices  $\frac{1}{|D_{b}|}\sum_{d\in D_{b}}\nabla L(\theta, d)\nabla L(\theta, d)^T$, regardless of the number of samples. 
The relevance of (5) was streamlined in $\text{(Le at el., 2022b)}^{[1]}$ , whenever all the tasks are trained using neural networks with the same structure, and number of parameters, and the distances between tasks (5) are comparable.

---

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
Dear reviewers,

Thank you very much for your detailed reviews and valuable feedback that significantly improved the presentation of our results. 

### Summary of Revision
Following the constructive advices from the reviewers, we have revised our manuscript as follows (all additional contents are written with red text): 
1. Major revision of the manuscript’s structure to improve the presentation
2. More explanations and intuitions for our theory and the proposed symmetrized task affinity (in Section 3, 4)
3. More details for the experimental results (in Section 5)
4. Additional experiments to compare symmetrized and unsymmetrized task distance (in the Appendix) 
5. Additional experiments to compare our approach with an extra baseline suggested by the reviewers (in the Appendix). 
---
Here are the clarifications to the common concerns.

### Novelty and Significance of Transfer Learning for Causal Inference
Transfer learning in causal inference is unique in the following manners: 
- Training data in causal inference tasks is typically more limited than the regular learning tasks. 
- The model’s Individual Treatment Effect (ITE) cannot be measured because no counterfactual data is available in practice. 
- Causal inference tasks exhibit a particular symmetry property (see more in the ‘Symmetry Property of Causal Inference Tasks’ section below) .	

---

### Significance of the Proposed Theory
A theoretical guarantee for transferring models is of fundamental importance because the model performance cannot be validated due to the absence of counterfactuals. 

There exists four important losses in transfer learning for causal inference problems:
- Factual loss of the source task (measurable)
- Counterfactual loss of the source task (unmeasurable)
- Factual loss of the target task (measurable)
- Counterfactual loss of the target task (unmeasurable)

While $\text{(Shalit et al., 2016)}^{[1]}$ has established the relationship between the factual loss and the counterfactual loss of the **same** task, our work connects the factual loss/counterfactual loss **across different tasks**. This work is analogous to the well-known regret bounds $\text{(Ben-David et al., 2010)}^{[2]}$ for discriminative classification models. To this end, we have shown that transfer learning for causal inference has a performance guarantee (i.e. regret upper bounds). This upper bound provides us with a sufficient condition for transfer learning in causal inference. Additionally, these regret bounds can be applied to any transfer learning framework that involves a pair of tasks.

---

### Importance of the Proposed Symmetrized Task Affinity
While these regret bounds indicate the transferability of causal knowledge between any pair of causal inference tasks, they don’t provide a constructive way to choose the **best** source task to transfer from, when multiple source tasks exist. **The order of performance of different models and that of their upper bounds are not necessarily the same**. Hence, we propose a label-invariant task affinity which finds the closest source task. Moreover, this task affinity satisfies the symmetry property (please see more in the "Symmetry Property of Causal Inference Tasks" section below) of causal inference tasks.

content.title: Continuation of the General Response
content.comment:
### Purposes of The Experiments
To verify the benefits of transferring causal knowledge and the efficacy of the proposed task affinity, we provide empirical evidence for the following results:
1. Transfer learning reduces the amount of training data for causal inference tasks by up to 95%. 
2. The proposed task affinity is a good indicator of the performance after knowledge transfer. It is observed to be highly correlated with counterfactual loss (which is not measurable in practice). Moreover, this correlation is observed to be robust to the model’s hyperparameters. 
3. The proposed task affinity successfully lends itself to the symmetry within causal inference tasks.

Please note that these experiments are not divorced from the theory and the task affinity presented in the paper. The theory demonstrates the transferability of causal knowledge and the first experiment shows the gain of transferring causal knowledge. On the other hand, the task affinity selects the closest source task, and identifies the symmetries within causal inference tasks. The last two experiments have corroborated these properties.

---

### Symmetry Property of Causal Inference Tasks
Causal inference tasks can be considered as having multiple regression problems, one for each treatment group. Given a source task, if we alternate the treatment labels (i.e., 0 to 1 and 1 to 0), the treatment effect (i.e., $\mathbb{E}[Y_1-Y_0|X]$) will be negated. Consequently, the non-symmetrized task distances $\text{(Achille et al., 2019; Le et al., 2022b)}^{[3],[4]}$ between the original task and the permuted task can be very large. However, the original model doesn't need to be retrained for transfer learning as we only need to permute the roles of output layers of the model in order to predict the individual treatment effects correctly for each group. In other words, the causal distance between these two permuted tasks must be zero. The proposed symmetrized label-invariant task affinity lends itself to this property of causal inference tasks. 

---

### Baseline 
Causal knowledge transfer is entirely new, and no clear baseline for comparison exists. Thus, we compared our method with one baseline (i.e., the training from scratch for the best model candidate).  Based on comments of Reviewers 8LDE and zZ6y, we also included the comparison of our results to models trained with bundled datasets, which further demonstrates significant gains of our approach. 

---

[1] Shalit, U., Johansson, F. D., & Sontag, D. (2017, July). Estimating individual treatment effect: generalization bounds and algorithms. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 3076-3085). PMLR.

[2] Ben-David, S., Blitzer, J., Crammer, K., Kulesza, A., Pereira, F., & Vaughan, J. W. (2010). A theory of learning from different domains. Machine learning, 79(1), 151-175.

[3] Achille, A., Lam, M., Tewari, R., Ravichandran, A., Maji, S., Fowlkes, C. C., ... & Perona, P. (2019). Task2vec: Task embedding for meta-learning. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF international conference on computer vision (pp. 6430-6439).

[4] Le, C. P., Dong, J., Soltani, M., & Tarokh, V. (2021). Task Affinity with Maximum Bipartite Matching in Few-Shot Learning. In International Conference on Learning Representations.
